I think Sanda, (which i'm a practitioner of) its really good, although lacks knees, elbows and clinch which i personally think is not 100% neccesary but is a really good tool, and sanda is not easy to find at certain areas.

On the other hand a good judo style can be super useful, because even though competitions dont focus on ground game, the martial art has ground on it and being an olympic sport is easier to find close to you, with the downsight of most judo dojos being mcdojos really.

Now, most mma gyms today do not teach a separate style or martial art, they teach grappling and striking for mma, and yes, there ks a difference, the only problem is that in some parts of the world like where i'm from (Mexico) an mma gym is not affordable, and thats what brings me to my next point.

I think one of the best combinations to have is wrestling (folk style, grecoroman style or freestyle) with boxing, both sports are easy to find, in most cases affordable, they give you a really round game and hard physicall cinditioning and if you can find a wrestling style with submissions like catch, S.A.W. or similars, i think its even a better option FOR MMA, But at the end its my opinion and if you practice any other martial art, is in you to make it work in mma with a lot of work and discipline. 😅

text:
I would go for Dutch style kickboxing rather than muy thai MT is a beautiful art with powerful kicks and strikes and heavy clinch work and ellbows, but it’s built around engaging in exchanges. You *communicate* with your opponent you kick, they kick, you block, they counter. It’s rhythmic and power-based, and you're grounded in close range.

Dutch kickboxing took the foundations of MT (especially the low kicks and ellbows and clinch) but evolved it into a faster, more mobile, in-and-out system. Dutch fighters are lighter on their feet, throw quick boxing combinations ending in low kicks, and rely less on standing and trading. It’s more pressure based and fluid, less about waiting for a return exchange.

Historically, the dutch actually trained in mt in the 70s then blended it with western boxing (which is always good) and kyokushin karate that’s why their footwork, angles, and combo flow are so different.

So yeah, MT might hit harder, but dutch-style kickboxing moves smarter.

So I rather go with that. I train it myself for years and I really like being mobile wouldnt trade it. Still I respect the power of muy thai trust me I do.

text:
What I always like to say is the best martial art is whichever one you can train, whatever is near you whatever you enjoy enough to stick around etc. And I agree that boxing has the best/most skilled hands of the popular martial arts and the arts I know, and I would agree that from what I’ve seen and done taekwondo has the most variety of kicks and the most skill in them, but I think Muay Thai gives you very solid skills in both worlds plus elbows knees and sweeps if where you train does clinch (which it should) so personally if you could only train one I’d recommend and train Muay Thai. I would like to add though that taekwondo now is more for the sport than not but I do wanna say that by no means do I think taekwondo and karate don’t work but I also do know that they are more sport focused than true battle in its roots (not granted all arts nowadays that are popular are primarily for sport but still) as that’s just the way it went in Japan at that time, still perfectly effective but just a note. (And that’s kinda the difference between jutsu and do which if I recall was like in the beginning of the edo period in Japan when they finally had peace they tried to restrict what combat training people could do with weapons and unarmed and all that so it became more sport focused but my memory isn’t the best and that’s just a side note ramble because I found it interesting when my kenjutsu (katana art the style I train is from 1336 I believe) sensei taught me that). But that being said most martial arts at least in the US train focusing on a 1v1 in a ring and say how you’d adapt it for self defense and hardly ever take into account deliberately training for fighting people of other styles of fighting and multiple opponents etc, but correct me if I’m wrong. Rambling aside I think for striking if you can only do one Muay Thai and striking is more important for say MMA or street defense at least in a situation where you have space but grappling is very important especially for self defense like if someone sneaks up and grabs you and for that my personal preference is jujutsu because it teaches you escapes from pretty much everywhere and most places nowadays will also give you a foundation of wrestling and judo at least where I train does. So the combo I personally train that I really enjoy and think compliments eachother well and gives a good foundation for them training other arts is Muay Thai and BJJ (plus I train balintawak a form of stick fighting and kenjutsu and hema which are two types of historical sword arts one being katana the other longsword and dussack) and those make me feel fairly comfortable in my skills with most weapons and situations but in my opinion variety is an amazing tool so it can’t hurt to at least dabble in many arts 
There’s always something to learn from everyone

1) avoid the fight/run if you can
2) if you MUST fight then strike first and strike hard and try to knock them out quickly. Try to stay on your feet and keeping your distance in case their friends join or they pull out a weapon.

text: This is what I hate about the Jiu Jitsu community. They are completely disingenuous. And I say this as someone who has lived and breathed Jiu-Jitsu for 25 years. Jiu Jitsu is not good for self-defense because there are so many intuitive ways to render most of what it has to offer moot when you are on the street with no rules. Try a double leg takedown on concrete. Try to lock something in when someone is ripping off your ear, biting you or poking your eyeball out. Jiu Jitsu does not work on the streets, and so many practitioners have learned this the hard way. Jiu Jitsu is foremost good for your mind, it can change your life in such a positive way but if you think you're a badass because you're a black belt and BJJ you're walking around with a great false sense of security.

text:
The question isn't which one is better in a versus, but which is better suited for a street fight. There are a few things to consider: Kicking above the knee is risky because your balance is more compromised, plus street dudes, not well versed in grappling, still know how to slam someone. 

Also, always assume +1 in any encounter. The last thing you really want to do is get into a grappling situation or even ground fighting (grappling) and their buddy starts stomping you into oblivion. So while grappling is more superior to striking in one on one confrontations (easier to close distance and neutralize strikes than to keep someone at arm's length), it is risky in a true street fight because you likely cannot finish someone with a single clean throw. With striking you have the potential to end it with your first punch. Grappling takes a few steps to get going.

So, out of the styles named, I'd pick boxing (no kicks) or Krav (anything goes mentality), with Muay Thai and Karate (Okinawan) as close seconds. But if I know for sure it's one on one, then all the grappling arts take the top spot, with Wrestling taking a slight lead (teaches you not to be on your back. Head slams into concrete are a possibility with Judo and BJJ ground fighting).

text: The real answer is that no one martial art or combat sport is strictly always better for every street fight, and the best way to prepare for a street fight is to train lots of different systems and pull the most effective bits from each of them as necessary. A lot of it depends on context. Some people’s strength is more optimized for striking while others have incredible endurance for grappling. Going up against a bigger opponent is very different than a similarly sized or smaller one. Getting ambushed is very different than having adequate warning. Going up against weapons is very different. Multiple opponents, unstable ground, and a million other variables. A good street fighter will train a stupid amount of different techniques as well as improving basic strength and conditioning.

text: Old school boxing is EXTREMELY Underrated. I’m talking about the likes of jack dempsey, jack Johnston, sugar ray Robinson, joe Luis era. Those guys fought in gloves made out of horse hair( they would thin out during the 15 round bouts ) so they where basically MMA mittens. To make long story short, those guys back than had a more mma friendly style where they didn’t rely on shelling up and eating shots of the guard they used more angles, head movement, footwork, worked the body more, and even the way they threw power punches was akin to MMA. But the biggest takeaway one can walk away from studying old school boxing is the grappling(yes that’s right) grappling for position, resetting, defense, set up offense, tire out opp, work the body etc… many gems from those old legends

It really depends...but from what I've experienced from Shotokan Karate so far, especially my Meeting with the Master which was BEYOND informative!
What I learned was that Form is Everything! He showed us how just a Tiny change in Posture, even just moviing 1 part of the body a couple Inches can change your Block or Attack from Weak, to Much Stronger than your "Body's Strength"...or with a Block, from falling apart to Withstanding the Toughest Blows...

I didn't ask him but I wouldn't be Surprised if he had a Degree in Something related to Bio-Mechanics! Because he really knows his Stuff! (Of course that should be a given when you are a 9th Dan Black Belt Master that studied under Canada's Karate GrandMaster).

text:
I laugh to myself every time I hear MMA referred to as if we're a style. MMA Stands for Mixed Martial Arts..it is by no means,  way or definition a martial art style or system. 
MMA was and is used to refer to tournaments that are not restricted to a single fighting style.
An MMA fighter could be trained in Boxing and TKD, or Judo and Sambo, or Ju-Jitsu and Shotokan etc. There is no syllabus,  ranking system, grading, belts, requirements when it's a mix of martial arts except within each of the individual arts. 
It's better and accurate to say you cross train in Judo and boxing for example, than it is to say you train MMA which by its very definition is an impossibility.
That's my opinion and I'm sticking to it.👍🥋

text:
If you wan to learn something for fun that’s fine, just be honest with what you’re learning it for, but don’t be fooled if you learn a martial art for self defense and the art doesn’t compete. You don’t have to compete but there needs to be a big enough of a pool of people who can test and prove the art actually works, if the art doesn’t compete full contact then it won’t work a lot of karate styles and nearly all Kung fu fall under this category. 

The reason people say if it doesn’t work in the  ring then it won’t work is because the ring, cage, mat, is where one can test and prove if a technique works or not, and if you can’t test it news flash it probably won’t work. You can apply some principles to some techniques  opening up your jab can turn into a nukite or adjust the hight of your front kick and boom there you have a groin shot; same with  a side kick to a joint kick. 

TMA guys need to quit coddling each other there are styles in martial art that work and don’t work and there are whole systems that don’t work. Sometimes it’s the practioners not sparing or competing (most of the time) and sometimes the art or style is completely useless (systema, ninjitsu, wing chun, tai chi, shorin ryu).

text:
The real risk of sunk-cost fallacy means that if people start in a useless martial art they end up feeling stuck in it even after realising it’s a waste of time and money. After investing so much on the road to a black belt, they feel they need stick with it to at least say they’re a black belt.

If they start in a martial art without a belt system, like boxing or wrestling, there’s no such problem. They learn something useful, can quit at any time and won’t have lost anything as the focus the entire time is on becoming effective in competing against other people, not a belt colour which in kids classes really has little value yet the kids are misled to believe it makes them effective fighters.

text: Good points. So many mistake the western worlds "sport/tournament karate for true traditional. Not the same. Traditional (budo) karate can't compete in these arenas it's not designed for that. Sort of like a Green Beret.  A bad dude right? Don't mess with him on the street. But how would he fare in the cage? It's not for that.  It's not about winning it's about not loosing. Even if I say  to my assailant "hey Look at that bird" and he looks away and I run and get away. I've accomplished my goal....he didn't.  It's just about survival and self defense. Of course you have to train for that properly .  On the more important side. Just training for self defense is only part of it. That can actually be done rather quickly if that was all you were after.  Traditional karate, however, is much more than that as you point out. It's about the real "self" defense....defense against yourself...sometimes your worst enemy. Constant improvement. becoming a better person.  So for example someone like me closing in on 70 years old. You think I want to fight? With my aches and pains? With my experience I'm hopeful I can do just enough to get away but I'm not thinking I'm anything special these days. However,  because it's traditional karate, I now have turned more inward and my practice is more moving meditation and constant improvement. We adjust with age. Sport? You outgrow it with age and then at some point stop.

text:
Great video!  I was an amateur boxer for a very long time and one of the things that stuck out the most to me was how different boxing gyms could have massively different "feels".  Sure we were all doing the same drills, same light and heavy sparring, but some gyms attracted a meaner crowd of boxers than others.  There were some gyms that seemed to attract students who were there specifically to learn how to hurt people.  These gyms were the worst because you couldn't trust your sparring partners. Plus violent people tend to have other personal and emotional problems, they are not good at hiding or keeping from effecting the people around them.  So actually learning to be a better boxer at these places was impossible. You can't spar if you don't trust your partner not to lose it midway!

The problem I have with MMA is the worry that an MMA dojo is more likely to attract the types of violent angry people that can turn the training floor into a dangerous volatile place.  And it seems to me that MMA schools purposefully try to attract this type of student and market themselves accordingly.

My problem with MMA isn't the style, it's the marketing and who they are trying to pull into their doors.

Well, strictly personal... MMA(basically Muay Thai, with added wresting) / Muay Thai(Kickboxing with knee and elbow blows), builds up body strength and focus(using simple straightforward techniques ofc) and most importantly, teach people how to take a hard punch or kick anywhere on the body!

text:
MMA was originally intended as a COMPETITION FORMAT to make possible the confrontation between various fighting specialities (just like how K1 was). I think this is misunderstood today, as many practice MMA as a "martial art" by itself, forgetting that it was originally a format that allowed anybody to use almost whatever technique was in their arsenal. Let's return to the original meaning of MMA: a way of testing and finding out what works, not to exclude any traditional art, rather to better everyone's understanding of what they practice - be it Kickboxing, Muay Thai, Wing Chun, Aikido, you name it. Even in training methods: muscle training is great, tendon training is great too, meditation techniques, breathing techniques - the world is very vast on this matter, and it appeals much more to me to discover those methods rather then criticize them based on the performance in a contest - which depend much more on the person who uses it then on the method itself - when I know nothing of it.
From an evolutionary point of view, it really holds more value - to me - to understand WHY people who went out in war practiced that way, and to take that point to evolve modern fighting, and at the same time re-introduce reality-based sparring mutuated from modern sports in methods that traditionally don't practice that way. 
That's my two cents on the question.

text:
I favor TMA over MMA, though it is also with an eye for aesthetics. MMA comes across as flavorless and bland, whereas TMA have a broader range of personalization, as opposed to MMA, which techniques seem statistics based and tend to follow a cookie cutter model (which is funny considering that is the MMA Perception of TMA).

I've blended different martial arts together, with my primary combination being sabre fencing and Taekwondo. I also implement aspects of things like Uechi Ryu, Aikido, and Sumo (more useful than it sounds) via observation (My technique in any specifically may be well below subpar, but I try to absorb aspects of their principles). Regarding my primary technique, however, I trained specifically in TKD for 20 years (since I was 4 until the day I tore my ACL at around age 24-25). During that period, I also studied Fencing for 7 years (1 year of foil, 6 years of sabre) completely independent from TKD, so those two are the most emphasized styles I blended.

Regarding technique gaps in TMA that seem as if they have no way of countering specific attacks or broader categories like grappling, chances are that the style does actually have counters to them, but are not often taught, which would make sense if the style was used in actual warfare (as it is adapt or perish). What's annoying with TKD (I studied the World Taekwondo Federation style) is that sparring is super wonky, and actually makes practitioners sloppy over time. TKD is often put up as a solely kick focused style, and a lot of that is due to what is seen during sparring (specifically that kicks to the head are legal, but punches to the head are not). The style does actually have a broad range of hand techniques. While I knew the hand techniques, I did not know how to implement them effectively until fencing. I don't punch like a boxer/kickboxer, but rather it is more like a fencing lunge. Rather than a long combination of strikes, I step deep in a manner akin to a lunge as I punch to impale. I actually had to hold it back during sparring as I often got accidental TKO's when training (the opponents crumple and drop for an extended period of time, even if protected by the padded torso protectors). My techniques are all taught in TKD, I just use them in a different manner (I suspect it would superficially resemble Chinese Kempo). I also use techniques that are seen much more often in any of the other aspects of the style, but never used during sparring - specifically the stances. Typically people rely on the fighting stance for everything in sparring, where I learned to flow through each stance as a result of studying fencing footwork. I've actually floored opponents simply through footwork and not even needing to land a hit.

The second question is a phenomenon I noticed while sparring that I can't quite explain, and was wondering if you had any similar experience. I noticed that from those in lower ranks all the way into black belts, opponents will tend to kick and punch at air a foot or two away from my body. I don't dodge, I just stand still and it happens. I am not sure if they are attempting to lead the target or if it is something else. It's happened about 20-30 times for me. There is also a more extreme version where I dodge as an opponent begins a flurry of attacks, stepping forward and slipping behind them. text: Mixed Martial Arts vs Traditional Martial Arts. It's a debate that been going on for decades over which one is "better". I practice a modified version of Laamb wrestling. I practice for self defense instead of combat glory. The Serer ethnic group was practicing Laamb wrestling for thousands of years. There Laamb wrestling was much more brutal than today Laamb wrestling, so there methods wouldn't work today for any society for the most part. However the people who practice Laamb wrestling today, there methods would go much better even in today's times, so long as it's a contest agreed upon. The same exact thing can be said for "mixed martial arts" vs "traditional martial arts". Would you say poking someone in the eye wouldn't work🤔🤔🤔??? Plenty "traditional martial arts" have such dangerous techniques, while "mix martial arts" hardly have any. Even though I can't tell you which martial art you should practice, (that's for you to decide) I can say it'll probably be better to stick with a martial art that best suit you. As a American, and a Sofa Knight,  I'm just giving my take on the martial arts. That's my story. Yera💧.

🔴🔴🔴Compared to boxing, MMA often acts as a refuge for those who are not good at real fistfights and lack the courage to face their opponent in a clean stance.

Why is MMA criticized as a "sport for incompetent boxers":

Lack of boxing technique: Most MMA fighters have a loose stance and chaotic punches without a hint of elegance. Instead of technical mastery, they rely on somehow "making" their opponent "feel good" because they wouldn't survive the first round in the ring with their fists.

Choking as a sign of weakness: Khabib's win over McGregor is a perfect example of this sporting wretchedness. Khabib didn't do anything special, he didn't show any dominant sportsmanship, he just hung on to his opponent and held him until he started to tear him apart. When someone can't knock out an opponent like a man with an honest punch, they resort to this primitive hugging. It's just a desperate attempt to avoid a real fight.

Misery instead of strength: Choking is the height of embarrassment in professional sports. It seems more like the attack of aggressive lunatics on the street than the performance of a top athlete. The fact that MMA rules allow something like this only proves that this "sport" has resigned itself to any aesthetics and honor.

Killing the viewing experience: Nothing ruins a sports broadcast more than two guys rolling around on the ground in some weird knot for ten minutes. It's boring, visually off-putting, and it completely lacks the dynamism that boxing has. The viewer wants to see power and precision, not someone crawling around on the ground looking for their opponent's neck.

Conclusion: Boxing is about character and facing your opponent head-on, knowing that your skill and toughness will decide. 

MMA is just a show of cowardly tactics, where instead of fighting, you run to the ground, which makes it a poor concoction of true sportsmanship.

text:
I lived in China for about two years to train full-time with various teachers. The main issue is the lost of understanding the traditional "meta". Sparring always frames itself arrow a certain meta, the game within the the game of what you are trying to achieve. If you're applying a kickboxing meta, then you'll be trying to get in shots, If its jiu-jistu you'll be trying to get the submission, in judo the throw, in MMA its usually a mix of the kickboxing and the jiu-jistu meta where you switch between getting strikes in and wrestling for submission.

So sparring is only good to train a certain meta, or fighting mentality. The issue is that very few people today can teach you a traditional meta or fighting mentality. Wing Chun for instance can not be applied with a kickboxing meta or jiu-jitsu meta, so if you learn Wing Chun moves but don't learn the meta where those moves are useful then you wont know what your doing in a fight.
Karate for instance is usually actually kickboxing, because the Japanese took the Karate movements from Okinawa but not the Karate meta, they learned the fight meta from the French kickboxing, so the Japanese Karate meta is actually like a bareknuckle Savate meta. Martial arts like Karate and Silat that have their origin in the larger Chinese martial arts culture and originally operate according the the fighting meta of southern Chinese schools (wing chun, white crane, bak mei etc.). The fighting method is based on achieving position and contact before expressing power at short range. This is typical for Chinese martial arts. The meta or mentality is like this: "I want to get a point of balance close to you before hitting you with my whole body force. In order to get close safely, I will use initial attacks, smothering, grasps and deflections in order to get my balance in a place that undermines my attackers balance, then I will strike with my whole body force."
Its hard to put into words, but hopefully the point comes across that there is a certain mentality with Chinese origin martial arts and traditional martial arts in general that you have to learn and develop through diverse methods of training if you want to apply the historical arts. Thank you.

I've been boxing for 15 years and are sparring partners for people who compete.  I started learning Wing Chun recently and have taken a few useful things from it:
- when fighting on inside, I will sometimes trap people's hands and use sticky hands to maneuver my fists to gain center line and punch to sternum or belly, which then gives my uppercuts as well.
- sometimes I punch through the high gaurd by not turning my fist (thumb facing up so the punch is thinner) which catches the opponent off guard, and sets up my other punches.

When I watch roberto Duran fight on the inside, the way he wrestles for the inside position is very wing chun-like.  

Of course it's not 100% true wing chun, but I draw a lot of inspiration from it.  And if course I can't use it all the time.  Need a good boxing foundation first

This is actually not even a "traditional martial arts vs modern martial arts" (subjective terms anyways) topic. It's actually quite simple:
1) learning techniques, is in general good for having a basis, but it does not teach you how to fight
2) to learn how to fight you need to test your techniques: know when to use which, when to attack, knowing which techniques will actually work (for you, because it can depend on the technique, but also on the person. Some techniques are more useful than others, but some people can also make some techniques work work super effective, while for others, that same technique simply doensn't work
3) testing techniques is not a matter of, trying the technique on someone else that is cooperating, no, it means: real sparring
4) addionally, to be able to fight, you need to be fit, strength, stamina, being able to give and take hits
5) if you really want to be "the best fighter", you need experience with both standing and ground fighting. This often means that 1 martial art will not be sufficient

The above applies for all martial arts. But some martial arts in general tick more of the boxes than others. But it is still heavily dependend on the school/dojo. There are also (kick)boxing classes for house wives and dads, where they don't spar, etc.
Also, not everyone has the same goals, not everyone wants or needs to be "the best fighter". But of course it is good for martial arts schools to not fake advertise and act like they are making you into "the best fighter", wil they only teach you some techniques without sparring, etc (like I think happens in Kung Fu a lot and in some lesser karate dojo's.

Also a lot of people don't want to work hard and put effort in something. So especially point number 4 they will minimize, but some will even minimize some of the other points. But this will of course make someone less "succesful". But again it all depends on the personal goals. Just don't full yourself in thinking you are a tough "invincible fighter" when in reallity, you are not.

Personally, for me, point 1, 2, 3, 4 are sufficient. And I prefer to limit the brain damage, so kyokushin karate is perfect for me. A LOT of body conditioning, both soft and hard sparring, but limited contact to the head (just kicks and knees, but in general you don't get continous kicks and knees in the head, since it's easier to hit someone to the head, than to succesfully kick someone to the head, unless your defense sucks) :D

I wouldn’t say they are dying, but every system has something to bring to the table. It just comes down to if the juice is with the squeeze.

A lot of traditional schools have issues introducing sparring because:

1) they are treated like a daycare
2) the clientele is generally not looking  for hard sparring
3) hard sparring can be very dangerous depending on the style and its intent.

The other thing to consider is the benefits of not hard sparring or doing so conservatively:

1) much lower chance of severe injuries like broken bones and TBI
2) able to spend more time on teaching technique and drilling the techniques to a higher proficiency level
3) the training lifespan of the practitioner drastically increases because they have been subjected to less bodily abuse

I think the appropriate training ideology falls somewhere in between the two extremes. 

Sparring / pressure testing time in a low-medium aggressive environment. This gives a chance to apply significantly more dangerous techniques in a training environment, as well as still triggering stress inoculation training. You can still do some hard sparring days here and there, just adjust the sparring parameters. 

Also understanding the likelihood of a positive outcome is much more likely if you train mindset. You could be the baddest boy in the block known by the best martial material, but if you are not mentally prepared for violence or willing to do violence, then you are a gardener in a war.

text:
I think points you really miss in this in this video are the question of "tradition" in itself and the question of usage and objective of the martial art.
Those "traditional" martial arts put the emphasis on keeping the tadition alive through the constant practice of the same customs and habits. That said, I agree that this make those martial arts partialy obsolete for real and contemporary fights.
But with this you understand that all martial art don't aim to be "street effective". Some maintain a cultural goal for exemple. Karate-do for exemple is often translated as "the way of the empty hand" as it was thought to be part of a more complete fighting system that included weapons that we call today "kobudo". Karate was meant to defend yourself when you didn't have any weapon on you. But if you had a weapon, you'd use it. This is noticeable in the form that traditional karate adopts : they are really similar to the forms you'd adopt if you used a weapon in your hands .
So you understand that modern martial arts answer to a different context : we live in a (relatively) pacified world where (most of the time) weapons are forbidden. In this world, yes, modern boxes are the best for an unarmed fighter against an unarmed opponent.
Take medieval japan : people at the time had a real necessity of mastering their techniques because they would go to the battlefield regularly. This logically conduced to different ways of practicing the training  but they used to train to combat realistically and the experience of the battlefield was even a stronger challenge for their fighting abilities. Try to use kickbxing against a naginata. However, japan's pacification and modern society made the samurai class die and their arts had to adapt too. This created Aikido and even Judo. 

So I agree to say that traditional martial arts nowadays are not the most useful in a street fight but that is not what they were made for and anyone who tells you the opposite is either a liar or an idiot. But at the end of the day a punch is a punch (especially in a street fight). Learning karate will still be better than doing nothing. Learning karate and traditional martial arts can be effective means of self-realisation and can bring fullfilment to one's life. I strongly believe this.

text:
Undated is probably a better expression than outdated. Because most traditional Martial Arts’ problem is actually that they LOST the tradition behind it. First, bare knuckle fighting was a national sport in Traditional Chinese MA. When you lost a fight, you might have to close your school! The government banned the fights. They also separated sparring from MA in the sport colleges. So that only ppl who do foreign MA actually spar. They killed it on purpose. 

Second, most of us seriously had no clue what we were doing. I mean that 100% literally. The traditional context has been lost. So that a spinning technique with the hands flying overhead, people think it’s a swing for more power… when it’s just a hip throw or an overhead throw. Even “masters” seriously think KungFu is meant to be like “Chinese Boxing.” No! Kungfu’s roots are Grappling with strikes, and with knives. 

Take something as simple as the fist to the waist “punch.” Just not understanding that the fist to wait is literally known as, “pulling hand” has people thinking it’s to generate power.

Chang Pu (Sumo Wrestling, but, before Sumo)  and Jiao Li (Military Wrestling) and Shuaijiao (Traditional Chinese-Mongolian Sport Wrestling) as well as a BUNCH of cultural styles like Shanxi style (No jacket wrestling) or local Belt Wrestling (similar to Korean Ssireum wrestling) this is Traditional CMA.

- Wing Chun guys stand upright and try to blast forward. If you meet a guy who is very good at Muay Thai Plum — that is what Wing Chun is supposed to look like, but, with more wrestling. Kind of like Sanda, minus the Tae Kwon Do influence. Ip Man’s senior brother, Yuen Kay San, learned Wing Chun from a Qing Dynasty constable (police chief). The Manchurian’s cultural martial art, just like the Mongolians, is wrestling. The Qing Army had ranked soldiers based on their excellence in Wrestling (“Shan Pu Ying”)

- Hung Ga.. Wong Fei Hung fought with the Black Army when they went down to Vietnam to help expel the french. If you notice, all the arts popular in Hong Kong / Guangdong all have 6.5 point pole / luk dim boon gwun. People think it’s a Wing Chun form, and it is not. 

- Yang Tai Chi. Yang Lu Chan learned some long fisted. Then learned Chen Family Martial Arts, it wasn’t called Tai Chi yet till his student named it that. Yang Lu Chan went and worked for the Manchu. See the above. That means his daily work as a trainer was against soldiers (wrestlers) and nobles (hence why you Push Hands and neutralize, rather than actually throw the person). 

- An art like Northern Praying Mantis, are literally from cities that are best known for their wrestlers. Gnaow, Laow, Choy these are all grabbing, controlling, and gripfighting.

- Ba Gua, people believe the myth that some Taoist was meditating in circles. No! BaGua was linear and zig zag pattern. Cheng Ting Hua had a wrestling sandpit where he trained. So, He had his students walk around the outside of the outer ring, while practicing their palm changes. 


Chen Tai Chi — Chen Wangting was a SOLDIER. General Qi Ji Guan and Yu Deyao document the soldiers training as Wrestling, Short Strikes, and Weaponry. Forms were not for fighting or shadow boxing, they were strictly a health promotion exercise for soldiers. That’s why you do most forms FAST. If we YouTube videos of Tournaments in Chen Village, it’s all grappling and throws.

These are the most influential arts.. and they’re totally lost almost.

Even once Sanshou started trying to “update” Traditional Martial Arts in the early 1900s, around the same era Judo was being developed, the govt of China ran joint exercise with Russian grapplers. They also had mixed martial arts matches in the 1920s. 

Okinawan Karate is White Crane KungFu and Luohan Kungfu as well as Taizu Kungfu, together with traditional Okinawan wrestling. The Bubishi, “The Bible of Karate” has around 36 techniques in it demonstated. Around 28 of them are grappling. Stand up grappling, single leg takedowns, escapes, even Ground fighting similar to the flying scissors or the imanari roll (which comes from Traditional Di Shu groundfighting).

So, Karate and KungFu’s problem is the opposite of others. Karate and Kungfu LOST their tradition. 

While on the opposite end, Judo and Muay Thai lost their self defense techniques because of the popularity of the modern sport.

text:
I'm a minute and a half in, it sounds like a shit take, but I'll hear it out.
EDIT 1: I'm at the sparring bit. You're comparing modern combative sports and techniques with old ones. Before you ask "would this work in a street fight" how about we ask "how long do I need to practice this for me to do it consistently against a resisting opponent"? To become basically proficient in Wing Chun it takes 6 months to a year of practice 5 days per week of a couple hours per day, for kick boxing it take 3-6 months of 3 times per week. This is pretty consistent with what I know of older martial arts, as masters would train the skillset for sometimes multiple decades, and they'd be good, sure, but that's not what we're dealing with when it comes to modern ones. Krav Maga was designed to be taught to an effective level in a few weeks. Again, kick boxing takes half the time to become familiar with the basics as Wing Chun and even competition levels of skill can be achieved in a few years. You cannot compare things like that and say "oh, the new one is destroying the old one". The new one was created specifically to fill a gap the old one couldn't, otherwise we wouldn't have the new one. Necessity is the mother of invention. 
EDIT 2: Also, sparring is probably one of the reasons you can build a base of proficiency so quickly, as it simulates an uncooperative opponent, and would better prepare you to truly fight. However, with the avoidance, many martial arts gyms these days have profit as the goal, not actually learning the martial art, and there are some places that simply check of that you attended the class for a certain amount of time to decide when you get your next belt. Profiteering and participation trophies are killing it, in my opinion.
EDIT 3: The purpose of the martial art is "not to compete" but to "defend yourself and neutralize your opponent"... buddy, are you insane? If you need to defend yourself on a street, someone can very simply stab you with a sharp stick, "were they able to utilize all the aspects" I really don't give a shit. If the martial art is effective it will continue to be so, so long as the practitioner has sufficient knowledge of it. If you meet on an even playing field(not a self defense situation where you may very well be at a disadvantage) and you lose, your martial art is not as good, or you, personally, as a fighter, are not as good. Those are the only two options. "Well, I didn't have space to wind up for the right kick to take him down because he was crowding me with jabs, but if I had, I would have one" is an excuse and is entirely unacceptable. You're telling me all I have to do to overpower your martial art is rush you? That means its a terrible way to fight. You can still have it as a way to build discipline, but if it is a fighting art, and its terrible at the fighting bit, that makes it just art. When its just art, anyone who wants to do art can pick up a paintbrush, people who want to become proficient at an effective fighting style will choose something else.
That is not how you convince me that the old styles aren't dying out because there's something inherently wrong with them. If I'm kick boxing and I lose a match vs a wing Chun practitioner are you really going to let me excuse my disgrace with a simple "well, I didn't get a chance to throw and elbow strike or a round kick, but if I had I would've won, so kick boxing is still better"? The answer is no, and if you even thought of saying yes, you need to go rethink your entire process and probably your life.

Keyboard warriors have a notorious reputation in the martial arts community for constantly claiming that traditional martial arts are outdated or useless. They flood comment sections with sweeping statements like "karate doesn’t work" or "kung fu is only for movies," despite never stepping foot in a real dojo. They act like self-proclaimed experts, usually backing their claims with cherry-picked clips or secondhand opinions from others who share their bias. Yet, when traditional martial artists actually win in real fights or competitions, these same critics suddenly go quiet—or worse, make excuses.
What’s especially ironic is that many traditional styles have deep combat roots and have evolved over centuries. From the precision of Shotokan karate to the deceptive angles of Wing Chun, these arts have produced skilled fighters who’ve proven themselves in various settings, including MMA. But keyboard warriors refuse to acknowledge this. When a karateka knocks someone out with a clean head kick, they say it’s "just athleticism." When a kung fu practitioner controls a street encounter, they claim it was “luck” or "the opponent wasn’t skilled." It’s never a fair win in their eyes—unless it confirms their bias.
This toxic mindset disrespects the years of discipline and training traditional martial artists put into their craft. Just because something doesn’t look flashy or modern doesn’t mean it’s ineffective. Real combat effectiveness comes from the individual’s understanding, timing, and application of their art—not the name of the style alone. Traditional martial arts have structure and principles that, when properly applied, can be incredibly effective in both sport and self-defense. But that nuance is lost on those who judge everything from a phone screen.
Instead of opening their minds, these online critics cling to narrow views and recycle the same tired arguments. They ignore evidence, downplay results, and dismiss anything that challenges their belief system. But time and time again, traditional martial artists prove that it's not about the style you train—it’s how well you train it. Until the keyboard warriors trade typing for training, their opinions won’t hold any real weight in the martial arts world.

The only way karate could officially have a "new move" is if some new guy founded a new style and included it in the curriculum, but if they did create a new style, the previous styles would frown and point the finger and say "heretics, unclean, excomunication!"

text: I trained in both judo and taekwondo simultaneously. If you go to a judo match you're not allowed to kick people in the face even though that's encouraged in a taekwondo match. Similarly in a taekwondo match I wasn't allowed to put somebody in an armbar or throw them into the ground. Part of sportsmanship is following the rules for the competition that you are in and not cheating or risking injuring people just to win. Using an illegal technique is a great dishonor to yourself and the sport and all of your training and all of those who have gone before you. Martial arts has one of the lowest injury rates of any sport because people follow the rules for the type of competition that they are in. Winning by using an illegal technique is a disgrace. text: I have never heard anybody say that traditional martial arts are useless. All martial arts stem from traditional martial arts. It is not a martial art that is slow, but the practitioner. The problem with mixed martial arts is that they are as the name implies, mixed. You can train in one martial art for decades and may never fully master it, though you would get good at it. If you try to train many at once the best you can hope for is to become a mediocre jack of all trades and master of none. As a handyman, a jack of all trades can fix many things, where as a master plumber can only fix plumbing, but can fix it better that than the jack of all trades. However in a fight to the death, mediocre dies at the hand of the master.  Training may be slow, because there are no shortcuts in getting good. Throwing a bunch of your favorite moves together and only learning those and calling it MMA does not prepare you for all situations. Most traditional martial arts have moves and techniques designed to handle a vast variety of situations however learning all of them in one particular art of style takes time and dedication. Doing 2 weeks of  training and paying exorbitant amounts of cash for a certificate that says you are a black belt as is widely practiced in the west, does not give you the skill, speed, stamina, precision, control and awareness that decades of repetitious training gives you. Doing ten pushups quickly lets you get them done in less time than doing them slowly, but doing them slowly builds more strength and stamina.

text: I really get tired of the whole "this fighting style is superior to the next". Ultimately they are all shit without training your body and experience to go with it. Heavy Weight boxers who are experienced and understand how to counter MMA styles can take them down easily if they can make a few solid connections which their fighting style specializes in. Military Navy Seals without all the fancy stuff can take down people who are traditionally trained, live eat and breath it because they have more practical experience. Having a real solid background will take you far, but only experience will teach you how to read a person, counter, and take down a person in the real chaos of a fight, and the more styles you encounter and learn from, the better you chance you will have to implement the style that best suits you against it. There are also always just going to be exceptional people, reflexes, agility, raw strength , you can train these to a point, but some people are just born different.
